The notification badge in the header always shows 0. Logging inside
proves the counter works: 1, 2, 3. The header re-renders every few seconds and reads

each time, yet never sees the new value. After an afternoon of debugging, the team concludes that imports are copies and starts wrapping every value in a getter function. The real cause is one line at the bottom of the counter module:
runs the module file and gives you a copy of its exports as they were at that moment. Two files importing the same module get two separate copies, and later changes in the module don't reach them.
, and in CommonJS that destructuring really does copy each property's value at that instant, because
returns an ordinary object. And the one case where ES modules do hand out a fixed value,
with an expression, looks exactly like a snapshot. Hit it once and the whole model seems confirmed.
A module's top-level code runs once, no matter how many files import it. MDN's modules guide says a module is only executed once, even if several

tags reference it, and the same holds for imports. In browsers, the HTML Standard guarantees it with the module map: it's keyed by the module's URL and type, and it exists so that imported module scripts are fetched, parsed and evaluated once per document or worker. Every importer gets the same module instance, so module-level state is shared app-wide. Imports are also hoisted: MDN notes that their side effects happen before the rest of the importing module's code runs.

content.text: The module map is keyed by the full URL, and the HTML Standard says queries and fragments aren't ignored. So
